china.intro:
China is a vast country where every region has its own cooking style, from spicy Sichuan to delicate Cantonese. Eating is central to daily life, and meals are usually shared at a round table.

This page explains what China is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
China is known for the Great Wall, the Forbidden City, the Terracotta Army, karst landscapes and fast modern cities. Its cuisine is often grouped into major regional styles, such as Sichuan, Cantonese, Shandong, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Fujian, Hunan and Anhui.

Tea culture, dim sum, noodles and dumplings are part of everyday life.

Peking duck, Sichuan hotpot, mapo tofu, dumplings, dim sum, hand pulled noodles and Shanghai soup dumplings are famous. Cantonese cooking favors fresh seafood and light flavors, Sichuan food uses chili and numbing pepper, and northern food uses wheat, with noodles, buns and dumplings.

Tea, soy milk, congee and street snacks start the day. Portions are often meant for sharing, so going with a group lets you try more dishes, and many restaurants have picture menus that make ordering easier.

Beijing offers the Forbidden City and the Great Wall, Shanghai has the Bund and modern towers, and Xi'an has the Terracotta Army. Chengdu is known for pandas and food, Hangzhou for West Lake, and Guilin and Zhangjiajie for dramatic landscapes.

Yunnan offers old towns and mountains.

The pace is relaxed and the climate is warm.

Fujian cooking is known for soups and seafood, with Buddha Jumps Over the Wall, a rich soup, oyster omelets, peanut soup, sea snail dishes and fish balls. Tea is served with meals, and street snacks include shacha noodles and thin pastry rolls called popiah.

Mushrooms, bamboo and fresh seafood are used widely. Portions are often meant for sharing, so going with a group lets you try more dishes, and many restaurants have picture menus that make ordering easier.

Xiamen has the Gulangyu Island, Nanputuo Temple and seafront walks. The Tulou of Yongding offer remarkable architecture, and Wuyi Mountain is a tea and scenery destination.

Quanzhou has ancient mosques and temples.

The local saying is that people here will eat almost anything, and meals are social events.

Dim sum, such as har gow shrimp dumplings, siu mai and egg tarts, is eaten with tea. Roast goose, char siu pork, wonton noodles, congee, steamed fish and clay pot rice are staples. Soups are slowly simmered with herbs and are considered healthy.

Desserts include sweet soups and ginger milk curd. Portions are often meant for sharing, so going with a group lets you try more dishes, and many restaurants have picture menus that make ordering easier.

Guangzhou has the Chen Clan Ancestral Hall, Shamian Island and the Canton Tower. Shenzhen has theme parks and modern architecture, and the Kaiping watchtowers are World Heritage. The Pearl River evening cruise is popular.

Hong Kong and Macau are nearby.

The city has green parks, beaches and mountain trails on its outskirts.

Because residents come from every province, Shenzhen offers all of China's regional cuisines, from Sichuan hotpot to Hunan, Hakka, Teochew and Cantonese. Look for dim sum, beef hotpot, roast goose and seafood. Hakka dishes such as salt baked chicken are local favorites.

The island has its own culture, with Li and Miao minority communities.

Hainanese chicken rice, Wenchang chicken, Dongshan mutton, Hele crab and Jiaji duck are the classic local dishes. Seafood is fresh and simple, and tropical fruits and coconut drinks are widely available. Qingbuliang, a cool sweet soup, is a favorite dessert.

Hainan coffee is grown on the island. Portions are often meant for sharing, so going with a group lets you try more dishes, and many restaurants have picture menus that make ordering easier.

Sanya has Yalong Bay, Dadonghai and the Nanshan Temple. Haikou has an old street and volcanic park, and Wuzhishan has rainforest. Diving and snorkeling are popular at Wuzhizhou Island.

The food is among the spiciest in China.

Chopped chili fish head, Mao's braised pork, smoked bacon, stinky tofu and dry pot are classics. Hunan cooking uses fresh chili and pickles, and dishes taste hot and sour rather than numbing. Rice noodles are a common breakfast.

Sweet tea and sugar cane drinks help cool the heat. Portions are often meant for sharing, so going with a group lets you try more dishes, and many restaurants have picture menus that make ordering easier.

The range of landscapes and cultures is large.

Yunnan food includes crossing the bridge noodles, a hot broth served with raw ingredients, wild mushrooms, rice noodles, goat cheese, Dai style grilled fish and pu'er tea. Flower petals appear in some dishes and pastries. Coffee is grown in the south.

Local ham and rose cakes are popular snacks. Portions are often meant for sharing, so going with a group lets you try more dishes, and many restaurants have picture menus that make ordering easier.

Lijiang and Dali are the main old towns, Tiger Leaping Gorge is a famous hike, and Shangri-La has Tibetan monasteries. The Stone Forest and the Yuanyang rice terraces are other highlights.

Tea and coffee shops are widespread. Portions are often meant for sharing, so going with a group lets you try more dishes, and many restaurants have picture menus that make ordering easier.

The Stone Forest, Green Lake Park, Yuantong Temple and Dian Lake are highlights. The Western Hills offer views, and the Flower Market is a colorful stop.

Tea is part of meals and relaxation. Portions are often meant for sharing, so going with a group lets you try more dishes, and many restaurants have picture menus that make ordering easier.

Hangzhou has West Lake and tea villages, Shaoxing has canals and wine culture, Wuzhen is a water town, and Mount Putuo is a Buddhist island. The Qiandao Lake is another scenic spot.
